## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Explain** regularization as a penalty on the size of the weights, added to the
  loss — a continuous flexibility dial whose strength (lambda) trades bias for
  variance. *(Understand)*
- **Contrast** Ridge (L2: smooth shrinkage, keeps every feature) with Lasso (L1:
  sparsity, automatic feature selection), and choose between them. *(Understand /
  Analyze)*

  and how model selection picks among whole model families by cross-validation.
  *(Understand)*

  features Lasso keeps. *(Apply / Analyze — in the lab)*

## Why This Matters

L09 left you with two tools against overfitting: a *referee* (cross-validation) that
**detects** it, and a *discrete* dial — pick `k`, pick `gamma` from a short list. But
the model itself was passive: you fit it, then judged it from outside.

Regularization moves the dial **inside the model**. You change the thing the model is
trying to minimize: instead of "fit the training data as well as possible", it becomes
"fit the training data well *and* keep your weights small". One continuous knob,
**lambda**, sets how much the second clause matters — and at the extreme, the model
will even switch some features off entirely. This single idea covers all three of
Unit III's remaining topics: how to tame a model (regularization), how to choose its
features (selection), and how to choose the model itself (model selection).

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
Think of fitting as packing for a trip with a **baggage fee**. Without a fee
(ordinary least squares) you stuff in every feature and let each weight grow as large
as the training data flatters — you "memorize" the trip. Charge a fee per unit of
weight and you pack only what earns its place. **Ridge** is a gentle per-kilo fee:
everything gets a little lighter. **Lasso** is a steep fee with a free-item threshold:
marginal items are left home entirely — the suitcase comes back with only the things
that mattered.
:::

## The Penalty Idea

A linear model predicts with weights $w_1, \dots, w_p$. Ordinary least squares (L03)
chooses them to minimize the mean squared error alone. Regularization adds a second
term — a **penalty** that grows with the size of the weights:

$$\text{Loss} = \underbrace{\text{MSE}}_{\text{fit the data}} + \lambda \underbrace{\,\text{penalty}(w)}_{\text{stay simple}}$$

Large weights are what let a linear model bend itself into knots through noise; taxing
them pulls the fit back toward something smoother. The knob $\lambda \geq 0$ (called
**`alpha`** in scikit-learn) sets the exchange rate:

- $\lambda = 0$: the penalty vanishes — you are back to plain OLS (maximum flexibility,
  may overfit).
- $\lambda$ large: the penalty dominates — every weight is crushed toward zero (the
  model goes rigid and underfits).

So **lambda is a flexibility dial**, exactly the kind L09 taught you to set — and you
set it the same way: by cross-validation. The two penalties below differ only in *how*
they measure "size of the weights", and that difference changes everything.

## Ridge (L2): Shrink Everything

**Ridge** regression penalizes the sum of the *squared* weights:

$$\text{Loss}_{\text{Ridge}} = \text{MSE} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j^2$$

Squaring punishes large weights hard and small weights barely at all, so Ridge
**shrinks every weight smoothly toward zero in proportion** — but never *to* exactly
zero. All $p$ features survive, each with a tamer coefficient. In the lab, Ridge pulls
the coefficient vector's length from 94 (at alpha=1) down to 53 (at alpha=50), yet all
30 sensors stay in the model. Ridge is the right choice when you believe **many features each
contribute a little**, or when features are **correlated** (it shares weight across a
correlated group rather than picking arbitrarily).

## Lasso (L1): Select by Zeroing

**Lasso** penalizes the sum of the *absolute* values of the weights:

$$\text{Loss}_{\text{Lasso}} = \text{MSE} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |w_j|$$

The absolute value keeps pressuring a weight at the *same rate* all the way down to
zero (the square's pressure fades as the weight shrinks). The consequence is dramatic:
as lambda grows, Lasso drives weak weights **exactly to zero** and leaves them there.
A zero weight means the feature is *gone* from the model — so Lasso performs
**automatic feature selection** while it fits. In the lab, Lasso cuts 30 sensors down
to 9, and then to 5, as you turn the dial. (Why exact zeros? The geometry is in the
Deep Dive.)

| | Ridge (L2) | Lasso (L1) |
|--|-----------|-----------|
| Penalty | $\sum w_j^2$ | $\sum \lvert w_j \rvert$ |
| Effect on weights | shrinks all toward 0 | drives some to **exactly 0** |
| Features kept | all $p$ | a sparse subset |
| Selects features? | no | **yes** (embedded) |
| Best when | many small effects; correlated features | few features truly matter; want an interpretable subset |

Can't decide? **Elastic Net** adds both penalties at once (a blend of shrink-all and
select-some) — named here, not drilled.

::: {.callout-note title="You have already met regularization: the C dial"}
L08's SVM and L04's logistic regression both carried a `C` knob. `C` is regularization
strength in disguise: $C = 1/\lambda$, so **small C means strong regularization**. In
fact scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression` is L2-regularized *by default*. The "lower C
if your SVM overfits" rule from L08 was this lesson all along — you were turning a
regularization dial before we had the name.
:::

## Choosing lambda: Cross-Validation, Again

lambda is a hyperparameter, so it is chosen by the L09 protocol — never on the test
set. Grid a few values, cross-validate each on the training data, keep the best mean
CV score, refit on all the training data, open the test envelope once. The lab does
exactly this and the CV curve peaks at a middling lambda — too little regularization
overfits, too much underfits, the sweet spot is between. (`GridSearchCV` automates the
loop; `RidgeCV` / `LassoCV` are built-in shortcuts.)

## Feature Selection: Three Families

Lasso is one way to end up with fewer features, but feature selection is a topic in its
own right — and fewer features means a simpler, faster, often better-generalizing, and
more *interpretable* model. The methods sort into three families:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  FS["Feature selection:<br/>keep the features that matter"] --> FIL["Filter<br/>rank by a statistic<br/>before any model<br/>(e.g. correlation)"]
  FS --> WRA["Wrapper<br/>train + score feature subsets<br/>(e.g. RFE)"]
  FS --> EMB["Embedded<br/>selection happens during fitting<br/>(e.g. Lasso)"]
```

- **Filter** — rank features by a statistic (correlation with the target, mutual
  information) and keep the top ones. Fast and model-blind, but ignores how features
  work *together*.
- **Wrapper** — train a model on candidate subsets and keep the subset that scores
  best; **Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE)** repeatedly drops the weakest feature
  and refits. Accurate, but expensive (many models).
- **Embedded** — selection happens *as part of* fitting. **Lasso is the headline
  example**: one fit, and the zeros tell you which features to drop.

## Model Selection: Choosing the Whole Model

Zoom out one level. The same L09 protocol that picks `k` or `lambda` also picks among
entirely different **model families** — linear regression vs a tree vs an SVM — and
their hyperparameters: cross-validate each candidate, compare mean CV scores, refit the
winner, test once. A useful split among families:

- **Parametric** models assume a fixed form with a fixed number of parameters — linear
  and logistic regression. Fast, interpretable, limited in shape.
- **Non-parametric** models let complexity grow with the data — kNN, decision trees
  (Unit IV). Flexible, hungrier for data, harder to read.

There is no universally best family; cross-validation on *your* data is how you choose.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Regularizing unscaled features.** The penalty taxes every weight equally, so a
  feature measured in large units gets an unfairly small weight and dodges the penalty.
  **Standardize first** (`StandardScaler`) — this is the moment L08's scaling warning
  finally bites. (Our lab's synthetic sensors are already on one scale, a deliberate
  shortcut.)
- **Selecting features on all the data, then cross-validating.** That leaks the test
  folds into the selection. Selection must happen *inside* each CV fold (a `Pipeline`).
- **Trusting Lasso's pick among correlated features.** Given two near-duplicate
  features, Lasso keeps one and zeros the other almost arbitrarily — don't read deep
  meaning into *which* survived. (Ridge or Elastic Net spread the weight instead.)
- **Forgetting that lambda = 0 is just OLS.** Regularization is a dial, not a switch;
  the un-regularized model is one end of it.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: why L1 makes exact zeros (Optional)" collapse="true"}

Picture minimizing the MSE subject to a *budget* on the weights (an equivalent view of
the penalty). Ridge's budget $\sum w_j^2 \le t$ is a **circle** (a sphere in higher
dimensions); Lasso's budget $\sum |w_j| \le t$ is a **diamond** with sharp corners
*on the axes*. The MSE contours expand until they first touch the budget region. A
circle has no special points, so the touch lands at generic coordinates — all weights
nonzero (Ridge). A diamond's corners stick out, so the touch very often lands *on a
corner* — and a corner has some coordinates exactly zero (Lasso). That geometric
accident is the whole reason L1 selects features and L2 does not. **Elastic Net** uses
$\alpha_1 \sum |w_j| + \alpha_2 \sum w_j^2$ — a rounded diamond — to get sparsity while
sharing weight across correlated features.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Ridge or Lasso — which do I reach for?"** — Lasso when you suspect few features
matter and want an interpretable, selected subset; Ridge when many features each
contribute a little or are correlated (Lasso would arbitrarily drop one of each
correlated pair). Unsure, or both? Elastic Net blends them and is a safe default for
wide, correlated data.

**"Does regularization always improve accuracy?"** — No. It helps when the model is
overfitting; on already-clean data it trades a little accuracy for simplicity. In the
lab, Ridge barely moves the score while Lasso both improves the test score *and* hands
you a 9-feature model instead of 30 — the simplicity is the win even when the accuracy
gain is modest.

**"What regularizes a neural network?"** — The same instinct, different mechanics:
**dropout** randomly switches off neurons during training (Unit V), and "weight decay"
is literally L2 regularization on the network's weights. The penalty idea scales all
the way up.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Regularization | add a penalty on weight size: Loss = MSE + lambda * penalty |
| lambda (alpha) | the strength dial; 0 = OLS, large = underfit; pick by CV |
| Ridge (L2) | penalize $\sum w^2$; shrink all weights, keep every feature |
| Lasso (L1) | penalize $\sum \lvert w \rvert$; zero out weak weights = feature selection |
| Elastic Net | blend L1 + L2; sparsity with correlated-feature sharing |
| C = 1/lambda | the SVM/logistic C you already used IS regularization strength |
| Feature selection | filter (statistic) · wrapper (RFE) · embedded (Lasso) |
| Model selection | choose families + hyperparameters by cross-validation |
| Scale first | the penalty is scale-sensitive — standardize before regularizing |
